doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: The war's end and taking his family west with Barnet
summary: Marty was not political; he was with Barnet at war's end and took his wife and baby daughter to California.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: When we look back on those times now, the end of World War II and we’re able to say okay well that was the demise of the big band, did you guys in the bands get a sense of what was happening at the time?
Well when did the business start to go downhill or to change for you guys?

Well to tell you the truth, in my youth I wasn’t very intelligent. All I had in my mind was playing the piano. I didn’t think politically, I didn’t think musically — well musically actually just for the band that I was playing with. And I didn’t know what was going on in the world actually. I wasn’t aware of all of those things. All I knew is I had to support a wife and a kid, and this is what basically took up time in my head. But funny you should say — the end of the war, I just looked at my book the other night and I noticed on 1945 when the war ended I was playing with Charlie Barnet’s band. We were playing someplace out in the midwest in an airplane hangar. I just read that the other day. Isn’t that incredible? I said look at where I was, with Charlie’s band, when the war ended. And we played a victory dance that night. It was great. But speaking about the war, with Charlie Barnet’s band we went, when we left New York, when we finished at the Strand Theater in New York, I had to make a decision because my daughter was just a year and a half old, and the manager said, “we’re going to go California.” I said, “gee I don’t know if I want to make that trip, I’ve got a wife and a little kid.” He says, “well you know every time we go to California, Charlie likes to sit down for about a year or more. I said, “that sounds good,” because he lived in Sherman Oaks, California, and when he got back to California he liked to sit there a while. In other words he was on the road then he comes home and he sits. So I said to my wife, and we had to make a decision, we were saying what should we do? In 1942 I was like 23 years old. And we said well let’s go. So we decided to go with the band. It was rough. Man, I’m telling you, I don’t know how, my wife and I think back and say how did we do it.
